items.question: How do you think about OpenAI as a counterpart to the Manhattan Project?
items.object: OpenAI as a counterpart to the Manhattan Project
items.answer: In the 40s the physicists went to the Manhattan Project. Even if they were doing other things, that was the place to be. And so now AI is the same thing, and I see OpenAI as that place. So maybe we don't need a public sector organized Manhattan Project, but it can be OpenAI.

And so now AI is the same thing, and basically said OpenAI as that place.
So maybe we don't need a public sector organized Manhattan Project, but it can be OpenAI.

rubrics.text: The response compares OpenAI's role as a focal destination for AI researchers to the Manhattan Project's role as a focal destination for physicists in the 1940s.
The response suggests that OpenAI could substitute for a publicly organized Manhattan Project for AI.

items.question: How do you explain your attraction to theoretical physics?
items.object: Theoretical physics as an expression of curiosity
items.answer: I think, and this is my stock answer at this point, but I think it's true: I was just an annoying three-year-old who never grew up. I asked why all the time, curious how everything works. I have a 19-month-old at home right now, and I can see the way he followed the washing machine repairman around and had to look inside the washing machine. I think I just kept that going. When you're more quantitatively oriented than not, rather than going to philosophy, I think you sort of veer into physics, and that was what interested me: does the world work? What is all this other stuff that's out there? The question that you didn't ask, but maybe I'll answer it ahead of time: the inward-facing stuff felt less quantitative and more in the realm of the humanities. So what is all this stuff that's pretty? What is all this other stuff in some of the same frameworks? That's been very exciting for me.

items.question: How did you view the good old-fashioned AI you encountered in your undergraduate AI class?
items.object: Good old-fashioned AI in his undergraduate AI class
items.answer: In undergrad I took an AI class, and it was very much good old-fashioned AI. A lot of the ideas in that class actually are coming back to be relevant, but at the time it seemed not very practical. It was a lot of, you know, if this happens, do that. There was also some game playing there that was sort of interesting. It was very algorithmic, but it didn't seem related to what it means to be intelligent.

items.question: Why do you see AI as a useful way to understand human intelligence?
items.object: AI as a way to understand human intelligence
items.answer: One of the things that's exciting to me about AI is the ability to have systems that do what humans do and to be able to understand them from, you know, what are the lines of Python that cause that system to do something, to trace that through and understand what are the outputs and how the system can see and classify: what is a cat, what is not a cat, or can write poetry. It's just a few lines of code, whereas if you're trying to study humans and ask what does it mean for humans to be intelligent, you have to go from biology through neuroscience, through psychology, up to other higher-level versions of ways of approaching this question. I think maybe, as a nice answer for intelligence, at least the things that are interesting to me are the things that humans do. And if you pull back the answer I just said a second ago, that's how I connected to AI: AI is taking pieces of what humans do, and we're understanding at least an example that's kind of simple and easy to study that we might use to understand better what it is that humans do.

items.question: Why did the statistical approach of machine learning change your view of artificial intelligence?
items.object: Machine learning as a statistical approach to artificial intelligence
items.answer: Yeah, actually it didn't click. I sort of wrote it off, and it would be great if there was a separation of 10 years between then and the next thing I'm going to say, but the writing off maybe lasted a year or two. Then I went to the UK for the first part of grad school. I spent a very long time in grad school, and I discovered machine learning and a more statistical approach to artificial intelligence, where you have examples of data, examples of a task that you want to perform. There are different ways that machine learning works, but you write down a very flexible algorithm that can adapt to these examples and start to perform in a way similar to the examples that you have. That approach borrows a lot from physics. I started grad school in 2009, discovered machine learning in 2010, and 2011 and 2012 was the big year for deep learning. There's not a big separation between write-off and rediscovery. Machine learning clearly existed in 2009; it just wasn't related to the class I took. This approach made a lot of sense to me, and it started to have real progress and seemed to fit in a framework that I understood scientifically. I got very excited about it.

items.question: Why do you think the methods of physics are well suited to studying large-scale machine learning?
items.object: Physics methods for studying large-scale machine learning
items.answer: I think the methods of physics are different from the methods of traditional computer science and very well suited for studying large-scale machine learning that we use to work on AI. Traditionally, physics involves a lot of interplay between theory and experiment. You come up with some sort of model that you have some theoretical intuition about, then you do a bunch of experiments and validate that model or not. There's this tight feedback loop between collecting data, coming up with theories, coming up with toy models. Understanding moves forward by that, and we get these really nice explanatory theories. The way big deep learning systems work has this tight feedback loop. The sort of math that we use is very well suited to the math that a lot of physicists are familiar with. I think it's very natural for a lot of physicists to work on this, and those tools differ from traditional theoretical computer science and theoretical machine learning tools for studying the theoretical side of machine learning. Maybe there's also a differentiation between being an awesome engineer and being a scientist, and tools from doing science are helpful in studying these systems.

items.question: How do you think statistical physics can help explain the relationship between a deep learning model’s individual parameters and its system-level behavior?
items.object: Statistical physics as a framework for understanding deep learning systems
items.answer:
There was a theory of how this works called thermodynamics, where—and I imagine everyone's seen this in high school—there's the ideal gas law that tells you there's some relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature. These are very macro-level things: you can buy a thermometer, measure the volume of your room, and buy a barometer as well. These are measurements that we use and talk about. Underlying this, and it took us a bit later to validate this and understand it, there's the notion of atoms and molecules, the air molecules bouncing around. We now understand that those air molecules give rise to things like temperature and pressure and volume. There's a precise way in which you can start with a statistical understanding of those molecules and derive thermodynamics, derive the ideal gas law from it. You can go further than that and derive that it's ideal because it's wrong; it's just a toy model, but there are corrections to it. You can understand from the microscopic perspective—the molecules, which we don't really interact with or see on a day-to-day basis—that their statistical aggregate properties give rise to this behavior we see at the macro scale.

To get to your question, I think there's a similar thing going on with deep learning systems. I wrote a book with Shada and Boris Hanin on how to apply these sorts of ideas to deep learning, an initial framework that allows you to start doing this. The micro perspective is neurons and weights and biases. When people think of the architecture, there are specific ways in which these things work: an input signal, which might be an image or text, and many parameters. It's very simple to write down, not that many lines of code, but there's a lot of weights, a lot of numbers that you have to know in order to get it to do something. That's the molecules perspective. Then there's the macro perspective: what did it do? Did it produce a poem? Did it solve a math problem? How do we go from those weights and biases to that macro perspective? For statistical physics, thermodynamics, we understand that completely. You could imagine literally applying the same methods to understand how the underlying micro statistical behavior of these models leads to the macro, or system-level, behavior.

items.question: How do you understand the gap in learning efficiency between humans and large language models?
items.object: Human learning efficiency compared with large language models
items.answer: The way humans seem to work at a similar scale to AI systems is much more efficient. We don't need to see trillions of tokens before we speak. My toddler has already started to speak in sentences, and he's been exposed to far fewer tokens than a typical large language model. There's some disconnect between human efficiency at learning and what large language models do. Of course, they're very different systems; they're designed differently, and the way in which they learn is very different, so in some sense that's to be expected. There's this gap here that you could imagine bridging.

items.question: How do you assess the scaling hypothesis as a path to the next steps in AI?
items.object: The scaling hypothesis and the need for ideas beyond scaling
items.answer:
What is the final GPT? There's GPT-4 right now, and it could be other companies as well, but since I'm going to join OpenAI, let me represent my new company. Is it going to be six? Is it going to be seven? At some point, assuming we have to scale things up, there are things that are going to break, whether economic—we're going to run out of, we're going to try to train a model that's larger than the world's GDP, or GWP, whatever the W stands for—or we're going to run out of GPUs, or we're not going to be able to put it... A lot of these things are going to break down at some point, and probably the economic one happens first. How many more iterations do we get before we run out of actually being able to scale practically, and where does that get us?

To tie those two perspectives together, scaling on its own—and of course it's impossible to disentangle this because people are making things more efficient—but you can imagine taking literally what GPT-2 was, which was the initial big model, and keep scaling it up. Is that going to get us to some super different, exciting economic power, or however you want to define the end state of AI research and AI startups and AI in industry? Or do we need lots of new exciting ideas? The general scaling hypothesis is that it's just the scaling and not the ideas that matter, whereas getting to efficiency like humans I think requires non-trivial ideas. To answer your question, the reason I'm excited about joining OpenAI is that I think there is high leverage in the ideas, in going beyond scaling, and that we will need that to get to the next steps.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between new ideas and scale in AI progress?
items.object: The relationship between ideas and scale in AI progress
items.answer:
I think there's this article by Richard Sutton called “The Bitter Lesson,” and it basically gives the argument that ideas aren't important, that scale is what you need, and that all the ideas are always trumped by scaling things up. It says a bunch of things, but maybe that's a high-level takeaway. There is a sense in which there were a lot of interesting ideas that came out in the 80s and 90s that people didn't really have scale to explore. After AlphaGo, DeepMind was writing a lot of papers, and people were discovering those papers and reimplementing them in deep learning systems. This was still before people realized, no, the thing you need to do is scale up. Even now with Transformers people are exploring other architectures or even simpler architectures that we knew before. Maybe scaling laws don't come from, as long as the architecture isn't sick in some way, having a special idea; they come from the underlying data process and having large amounts of data. I think the real answer is that there's a balance between the two: scale is hugely important, and maybe it was just not understood how important it was. We also didn't have the resources to scale things up at various times. There's a lot of parts along the supply chain or product chain in order to make those GPU clusters happen and deploy them. GPUs have co-evolved to be well suited for these models. In some sense Transformers was a good idea because it was designed to be well suited to train on the systems we had at the time. These other architectures could do it at an ideal scientific level, but at a practical level it was important to get something able to reach that scale.

I still think ultimately someone came up with the idea of deep learning; that was an important idea. Pitts and McCulloch came up with the original idea for the neuron, and Rosenblatt came up with the original perceptron. There are a lot of people going back 80 or so years making important discoveries that were ideas that contribute. It's easy to see how, if you're bottlenecked and then all of a sudden you get to apply, people think about ideas; then if you unlock a new capacity of scale somehow, you see a huge set of results and it seems like scale is super important. I really think it's more of a synergy between the two.

items.question: How do you see OpenAI potentially filling the role of a Manhattan Project–scale organization for AI?
items.object: OpenAI as a Manhattan Project–scale organization for AI
items.answer: Well, one thing I can say is that part of the process that led me to OpenAI is I was talking with your partner Sean Maguire, who brought me to Sequoia in the first place, and trying to figure out: is there a startup that makes sense for me to work on that has the right mix of scientific questions, research questions, and also as a business? I think it was Sean that said—and I don't mean the analogy in terms of the impact, in terms of the negative impact of what you might think of the Manhattan Project, but just in terms of the scale in the organization—he said, “In the 40s the physicists went to the Manhattan Project, even if they were doing other things. That was the place to be. And so now AI is the same thing.” He basically said OpenAI as that place. So maybe we don't need a public-sector-organized Manhattan Project, but it can be OpenAI.

items.question: Why do you think we can scientifically understand complex AI systems?
items.object: Scientific understanding of AI systems
items.answer: I think within AI communities, my contrarian position is that we can really understand these systems. Physics systems are extremely complicated, and we have made a huge amount of progress in understanding them. I think these systems sit in the same framework. Another principle that Shada and I talk about in our book, a principle of physics, is that there's often extreme simplicity at very large scales, basically due to statistical averaging or, more technically, the central limit theorem. Things can simplify. I'm not saying this is what happens exactly in large language models, of course not, but I do think that we can apply the methods that we have, and hopefully have AI that can help us do this in the future. By AI I mean tools, not individual intelligences just going running on their own and solving these problems. I guess I feel at the extreme end that this is not going to be an art, that the science will catch up and we'll be able to make extreme leaps in really understanding how these systems work and behave.

items.question: How do you think working on AI could become the highest-leverage way to answer a physics question you care about?
items.object: Working on AI as a way to accelerate physics research
items.answer: I'm definitely optimistic. I still have a lot of friends that work in physics, and there's a growing sense, maybe even approaching a dread—and maybe this is actually the answer to why physicists work on AI—that if what you care about is the answer to your physics question and you want to make it happen as soon as possible, what is the highest-leverage thing you can do? Maybe it's not work on the physics question you care about, but work on AI because you think AI might end up solving those questions very rapidly anyway. I don't know the extent that anyone really takes it seriously, but within the theoretical physics community I come from, this is a thing that gets thrown around and discussed.

items.question: Why do you see AI's success at games as grounds for optimism about mathematical discovery?
items.object: Inference-time compute and mathematical discovery
items.answer: My perspective is that math will be easier than physics, which maybe betrays the fact that I'm a physicist, not a mathematician. I think what's exciting about math is that we made a lot of progress in terms of solving games by doing more than just looking up what strategy we should use to play the games, but also being able to simulate forward. The way that if I'm in a very hard position in a particular game, rather than just playing with intuition, I might sit and think about what I should do. Sometimes this goes under the name inference-time compute rather than training-time compute or pre-training. There's a sense in which what it means to do reasoning is very related to this ability to sit and think. We know how to do it for games because there's a very clear winning and loss signal, so you can simulate ahead and figure out what it means to do good or not. I think math, in some parts of math—again, I'm not a mathematician, and I'm always scared about talking about math publicly and saying something wrong that will upset mathematicians—seems like certain types of math problems are not as constrained as games, but are still constrained enough where there's a notion of finding a proof. items.question: How do you think helping physicists with AI differs from building AI systems that solve mathematical proofs?
items.object: AI for physics research compared with AI for mathematical proofs
items.answer:
I think some of the flavor of what physicists care about and doing physics feels a little different—this is where I might get in trouble—than some of the mathematical proof-type things. Physicists are known to be more informal and hand-wavy, but also, on the other hand, connected to the interplay between experiment and the sort of models that physicists study. Maybe what saves them is that things are informal and hand-wavy but very explanatory. Like we were saying earlier, the engineers discovered all the exciting industrial machines, then the physicists maybe cleaned up a bunch of the theory about how that works, and then the mathematicians come later and clean it up, formalize everything even more. There are mathematical physicists that clean up a lot of it, make it proper, and try to understand in formal ways some of the stuff physicists do.

I think the key point is that the sort of questions interesting to physicists maybe don't look like proofs. Maybe it's not about how, given a particular model, do we actually solve it. Once things are set up correctly, people trained in the field are able to figure out how to analyze those systems. It's more the other stuff: what is the right model to study? Does it capture the right sort of problems? Does this relate to the thing that you care about? What are the insights you should draw from it? For AI to help there, I think it would look different than the way we're trying to build AI systems for math. Rather than “here's the word problem, go and solve this high-school-level problem” or “prove the Riemann hypothesis,” the questions in physics are like, “What is quantum gravity? What happens when something goes into a black hole?” That's not like, start generating tokens on that. What does that even look like? If you go to a physics department, people hang out at the blackboard, they chat about things; maybe they sketch mathematical things, but there are a lot of other things that go into this. Maybe the data you need to collect looks more like that, or maybe it looks like the random emails and conversations on Slack and the scratch work.

items.question: How do you see AI tools fitting into scientific research across different fields?
items.object: AI tools for accelerating scientific research
items.answer: There are definitely tools we can use, like “help me understand this new paper so I don't have to spend two weeks trying to study it and understand it,” maybe let me ask questions about it. I think there are problems with the way that's currently implemented, but there are a lot of tools that will help accelerate physicists, just like Mathematica, a software package that does integrals and a lot more than that. I use it to do integrals, and sometimes it doesn't know integrals, and you can look them up in integral tables. This applies to other branches of science too. The ways in which the questions are asked and what it means to do science in different fields can look further and further from games. To the extent that's true, we'll need lots of ideas, but we'll have to approach them all differently. Maybe eventually we'll have a universal thing that knows how to do all of it, but initially a lot of these things feel a little different from each other.

items.question: Why do you see mathematics and physics as relatively easy domains for AI compared with biology?
items.object: The relative difficulty of mathematics, physics, and biology for AI
items.answer:
I'd push back and say, well, it's not hard; these are the easy domains. I'm bad at biology, but it doesn't make any sense to me at all. My girlfriend is bioengineering and in biotech, and what she does just makes no sense to me; I can't understand any of it, whereas physics makes complete sense to me.

I think maybe a better answer, or a less global answer, is that, like I was trying to say about math, there are constraints. In particular with math, a lot of it is unembodied. You don't have to go and do experiments in the real world. They're self-sufficient, and that's close to generating text, the way language models work, or even the way some reinforcement learning systems work for games. The further you go from that, the messier things become, and the harder it probably is. It's also harder to get the right kind of data to train these systems. If you want to build an AI system that solves biology, people are trying to do this, but it seems difficult. I guess you need to also make sure robotics works so it can do those sorts of experiments, and it has to understand that sort of data, or maybe it has humans do it. For a self-sustaining AI biologist, it seems like there are a lot of things that are going to go into it. On the way we'll have things like AlphaFold 3, which just came out, and which I didn't get a chance to read the details of, but I saw that they're trying to use it for drug discovery. I think each of these fields will have things developed along the way, but the less constraints there are and the messier and more embodied it is, the harder it will be to accomplish.

items.question: How do you think about the distinction between one AI model that understands everything and a collection of domain-specific models?
items.object: The distinction between one general AI model and a collection of specialized models
items.answer: What does it mean to be different? There's a trivial way to make the question meaningless, by saying the model is the union of all those other models. But there's also a sense in which mixture of experts is not what it was originally meant to be; it's not that in practice at all. There's a sliding scale here. It does seem like people, at least the big labs, are going for the one big model and have a belief that that's—I don't know, but maybe I will in the future understand what the philosophy is there.

items.question: How do you imagine AI development changing over the next five years as scaling runs its course?
items.object: AI scaling and the next five years of AI development
items.answer: So it seems like for the last five years we've been doing scaling. I imagine within the next five years we'll see that scaling will terminate, and maybe it will terminate in a utopia of some kind that people are excited about. We're all post-economic and so forth, and we'll have to shut down all your funds and return Monopoly money because money won't matter. Or we'll see that we need lots of ideas; maybe there will be another AI winter. I imagine something will be interestingly different within five years about AI. It might just be that AI is over and we're on to the next exciting investment opportunity, and everyone else will shift elsewhere. I'm not saying that's what's motivating me about AI, but maybe five years is enough time to see that.

items.question: What do you hope to learn from the next generation of AI models?
items.object: Progress between successive generations of AI models
items.answer: I'm excited to learn what's exciting at the forefront of a huge research lab like OpenAI. One thing that'll be interesting will be the delta between the next generation of models. There are ways in which things are scaling up in terms of—I guess it's not really public aside from Meta—in terms of size of data, size of models. We see scaling laws, and scaling laws relate to something like the loss, and it's hard to translate that into actual capabilities. What will it feel like to talk to the next-generation model? What will it look like? Will it have a huge economic impact or not? In terms of estimating velocity, you need a few points; you can't just have one point. We sort of have that with GPT-3 to GPT-4, but I feel like with the next delta we'll get to really see what the velocity looks like and what it feels like going from model to model to model. Maybe I'll be able to make a better prediction five months from now, but then I probably won't be able to tell you guys.

items.question: Why do you deliberately use humor and informality in your technical writing?
items.object: Humor and informality in technical writing
items.answer:
It's definitely deliberate. It goes into—I think in some sense it's inherited. I mean, I definitely am a not-serious person, but I also think it's inherited from the style of the field that I came from. I'll tell you a story. I was a postdoc at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and I was having lunch and joking around with this professor, Nati Seiberg, who's a professor at the Institute. Then we got into—I think we were talking about someone asked the question about what is a good title, and I was like, “Oh, the title has to be a joke,” and he was on board with that. Then I was explaining that for me the reason to write a paper is for the jokes: you have a bunch of jokes in mind, and then you want people to read those jokes, so you have to package it into the science product, and people want to read the science product and they're forced to suffer through the jokes. He's this Israeli professor, and he was like, “I don't get it. Why can't you just do the science? Why do you need the jokes? The jokes are great too, but you should write for the science, not for the jokes.” I was adamant that I write for the jokes.

I think at some point you learn about the scientific method and the formal ways of doing things and all these rules, and then you grow up a bit. Maybe I had a roommate who is a linguist, now a professor of linguistics at UT Austin, and he emphasized that he could tell me which rules I could break, where the rules come from, and why they're important or not. You realize that you can break these rules, and the ultimate goal should be: is the reader going to read it and understand it and enjoy it? You don't want to do things that compromise their ability to read and understand, but you don't want to obscure things. If it's more enjoyable, people are more likely to read it and take the point. It's also more fun if you're writing it. I think that's where that comes from.
